articles.title: The giant pre-historic insect found by miners
articles.summary: Griffinflies, a dragonfly-type insect, ruled the skies millions of years before the dinosaurs.
articles.body:
Before dinosaurs roamed the Earth, seagull-sized dragonfly-like insects known as griffinflies ruled the skies.

More than 300 million years later, miners unearthed two fossilised remains of the "gigantic" insects 500m (1,640ft) below the surface at Bolsover Colliery, in Derbyshire, in 1979.

The only known remains of whalleyala bolsoveri, with a 17.4cm wingspan, and arctotypus diluculum, believed to have had a wingspan of about 50cm, were discovered and are now housed at London's Natural History Museum.

The two "irreplaceable" specimens, dubbed the "Bolsover Dragonflies", are the only known example of the species ever to be found, according to the museum.

With a sculpture of the Bolsover Dragonfly set to be unveiled on a roundabout in the town on Monday to celebrate the discovery, what are griffinflies and how did they end up in Derbyshire?

Local historian and archaeologist Dr Simon Elliott said the "Bolsover Dragonflies" lived during the Carboniferous period, between 359 and 299 million years ago.

"The key thing is the environment in Bolsover was wet and swampy," Elliott explained.

"This period had the first reptiles on land, the first fish and a number of insects that already existed from earlier periods of history."

The Natural History Museum said griffinflies were "ferocious hunters" that would eat "anything and everything they can find".

Similar to dragonflies, griffinflies are described by the museum as the "large, extinct cousins of both dragonflies and damselflies".

"If it was in Jurassic Park, people would be running," Elliott said.

As well as giant dragonflies that had wingspans up to 71cm (2ft), the landscape was filled with poisonous centipedes that were 2m (6ft) long, as well as cockroaches and scorpions that were 1m (3ft) long.

The museum said giant insects were able to grow so large because vast forests removed huge amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, increasing oxygen levels to about 35%, compared with 21% today.

Over time, dragonfly-like insects became smaller and faster because birds, which evolved from dinosaurs, emerged as new predators.

Elliott said north Derbyshire and surrounding areas became key coal mining sites because of vast forests of bark-bearing trees that grew during the Carboniferous period and later formed large coal deposits.

The 61-year-old said the Bolsover Dragonflies would have died and fallen into the wet ground, which was "the key to it later becoming a fossil".

The layer of Carboniferous land was later covered by shallow seas from the Permian period, between 298.9 and 251.9 million years ago.

"The fossils were found 500m underground because miners had to dig through all the Permian magnesium limestone that covers Bolsover to reach the older coal seams below," said Elliott.

Richie Howard, curator of fossil arthropods at the Natural History Museum, said the Bolsover Dragonflies were so rare they were not currently exhibited in the public galleries.

"They are, indeed, the only known example of those species. No more have ever been found of either of them and, as the colliery is no longer active, probably no more ever will be," said Howard.

"Specimens of this nature are not usually exhibited because they would be irreplaceable if damaged or stolen."

Howard said whalleyala bolsoveri was discovered by a miner called Malcolm Spencer, while the arctotypus diluculum was found by another miner called Graham Ball.

The whalleyala bolsoveri is the "smaller" of the two specimens, said Howard.

The arctotypus diluculum, formerly named tupus diluculum, is the "larger" of the two specimens, but was incomplete and in "several fragments".

A sculpture of the "Bolsover Dragonfly" is being unveiled on a roundabout at the junction of Chesterfield Road, Riverside Way, Intake Road and Station Road on Monday.

It was made by school students in the area who took part in a 20-week programme to learn metal cutting, design, and welding.

Bolsover District Council leader Jane Yates said the sculpture was a "great source of pride for Bolsover".

"I find it fitting that the sculpture is overlooked by Bolsover Castle, making it a real focal point for people entering the town," she said.

"What makes this sculpture even better is that it was created by young people who have been given a chance to learn skills for life.

"I hope this sculpture remains here for many years to come."

articles.title: Gunman who killed at least 6 in Kraków mass shooting has died in hospital
articles.summary: A gunman who killed at least six people during a deadly rampage in the Polish city of Kraków on Saturday has died in hospital, Reuters news agency reported on Monday, citing police.
articles.body: A gunman who killed at least six people during a deadly rampage in the Polish city of Kraków on Saturday has died in hospital, Reuters news agency reported on Monday, citing police. The country was horrified by the rare mass shooting in the historic main square of the city in the country’s south, which prompted national mourning and heightened security, as authorities said the attack was likely driven by far-right ideology. The Polish citizen, in his 20s, was shot and injured by police during the attack before being transported to hospital. There, he underwent multiple surgeries and had been in a critical condition prior to his death. The mass shooting — which authorities said they are investigating as a possible terror attack — has generated a wave of fear in a European nation with exceptionally tight gun laws. Kraków police said the gunman drove into the city’s main market square, typically popular with tourists and locals, and started firing randomly at people, initially from his car, killing four women and two men, on Saturday afternoon. Sixteen others were injured, including two police officers. The alleged attacker was wearing military-style clothing and used “military weapons,” Police Deputy Inspector Katarzyna Cisło told Polish news outlet TVN24. Weapons and ammunition were also found in his vehicle. The bodies of his sister, mother and father were later found at the suspect’s home in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 120 miles northeast of Kraków. Poland’s prosecutor’s office said Sunday that it is “highly likely” the killings were carried out by the same person, but investigations were ongoing. Eleven firearms were recovered from both sites, the prosecutor’s office spokesperson said. Gunman’s clothing examined Little is known about the gunman, who has not been identified by police, and his motive was not immediately clear. But Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said that the shooter was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical views.” Emblems on his clothing were being examined by experts, an interior ministry spokesperson said on Monday. “These patches were associated with various motifs that are currently being analyzed by specialists,” Karolina Galecka told radio TOK FM, Reuters reported. The suspect was a member of a shooting club and appeared to be highly skilled marksman, the club spokesperson Adam Chyb told Reuters on Sunday. Poland, like other European Union countries, has strict rules about acquiring guns and very few people are allowed to own military-style weapons or carry guns in public. About 411,000 people have gun permits in the country, which has a population of more than 37 million, according to the Associated Press. Off-duty surgeons saved lives An off-duty surgeon who rushed to the scene of the shooting to treat victims of the attack, including a police officer, said he had just finished eating lunch with his family when he heard “what sounded like gunshots.” Michal Pedziwiatr described being “in the eye of the storm” as he and a friend – also a surgeon – began providing care to the wounded. Pedziwiatr told a press conference on Sunday that his friend, Mateusz Wierdak, was a “hero” for saving the life of a police officer who subdued the attacker, after he “applied pressure to the bleeding wound without any protective gear or gloves” and “stuffed gauze pads into the chest cavity,” Reuters reported. The two wounded police officers, who Polish Prime ​Minister ‌Donald Tusk praised for also saving “many lives,” underwent surgery and remain in hospital, police said. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Telford Theatre demolition to continue as plans approved
articles.summary: Contractors will now start getting the site ready for further demolition, the council says.
articles.body:
Work to demolish a town's cinema can continue after upgraded plans for the site were approved.

Telford Theatre, in Oakengates, is being fully demolished and replaced as the original building, dating back to the 1960s, has "significant structural defects".

The newly-approved plans from Telford and Wrekin Council include a new entrance foyer and box office, larger community and rehearsal spaces, bigger bar areas and additional toilets.

The council has also finalised the purchase of land next to the theatre's car park, which will create more than 30 extra spaces.

Contractors are due to begin site enabling works on Monday to extend barriers around the demolition site.

New facilities at the theatre will include a 766-seat auditorium, studio theatre, and community art room.

Twelve full-time jobs will be created as well as some part-time roles. About 100,000 visitors a year are expected.

The original plans for the development were upgraded and resubmitted for approval after the demolition of the previous theatre on the Oakengates site revealed there was extra space to expand into.

Lee Carter, leader of the council said: "We are delighted that the upgraded plans for the new theatre have now been approved enabling the remainder of the demolition works to begin, which in turn will pave the way for the new theatre rebuilding project.

"Telford Theatre is an eagerly anticipated project throughout Oakengates and wider community and it's one of our biggest investment projects across the Borough."

The project is part of a wider regeneration of the Oakengates area which includes refurbished shops and a paved events area outside the theatre.

articles.title: 'I smashed my dead brother's belongings in a rage room'
articles.summary: From bereavement to stillbirth, more women are finding release in rage rooms from Bath to Swindon.
articles.body:
When Ellie Goudie's brother Ryan died aged 23, she could not bear the thought of anyone else having his belongings.

Instead, she paid to smash them to pieces.

Armed with a baseball bat in a Swindon rage room, Ellie destroyed some of the possessions Ryan had left behind, including his beloved television, saying it helped her cope with the pain of losing him.

"That was his. He can't have it any more, so no one should," she said.

For Ellie, the experience was about far more than breaking objects.

"I felt Ryan in here. He probably was doing it with me," she said. "I'm glad I've done it for him."

Ellie is one of a growing number of women turning to rage rooms, where customers pay to destroy household items with baseball bats and crowbars in a controlled environment.

Operators say many visitors are seeking an emotional release during some of the most difficult periods of their lives, including bereavement, trauma, relationship breakdowns and stress.

At The Rabbit Hole Rage Room in Swindon, owner Paul Bunney said about 70% of customers are women.

He said he sees a visible change in people after they come out of a session.

"Some people are quite reserved when they come in, and then when I go and speak to them after they have a big smile on their face." he said.

"They're hot, they're sweaty, and they've got rid of a lot of emotion."

Visitors travel from across the region to take out their rage on objects that were destined for landfill, like printers, crockery, hifi systems, kettles and old wine bottles.

Paul said materials are often separated and recycled afterwards.

For Ellie, the attraction was the sense of release she felt after months of grief.

"You're taking out your anger and you don't have to talk," she said.

"It takes away the emotion for the good hour or so you've got in here. And then you feel a relief when you come out

A similar story has emerged at another rage room in Bath.

Charlotte Bagnall, who runs Raging Bath, said what began as a fun attraction had developed into something much more meaningful.

"I think everyone at the moment needs release," she said.

"When you're here, you can just let go."

She said many customers arrive carrying emotional burdens they have struggled to process elsewhere.

"The people I've got to meet and the things they go through is fascinating, but also quite sad at times.

"To lighten that load they're carrying is huge."

Among them is Ceri Crannis, who booked sessions for her family after her daughter was stillborn.

She said the experience provided something she had struggled to find elsewhere.

"You don't get that release in therapy when you're talking," she said.

"There are some things that are just so deeply hidden that it comes out here, where loud music, smashing, breaking really does just hit the spot where nothing else has managed to do that before."

Ceri believes rage rooms can offer women a rare opportunity to express emotions that are often suppressed.

"Social norms are geared up that women are well behaved, they don't swear, you don't break anything."

Another rage room visitor, Sarah Bear, agreed.

"You can't shout and scream at the people in the world because actually those people have done nothing wrong, but you can take it out on stuff here that isn't going to hurt anyone," she said.

"So it's a really safe, controlled way to do it. And yeah, there might be some tears at the end of it, as, like, the relief washes over us, but it's worth it."

It's no surprise that rage rooms can offer an immediate feeling of relief, according to associate professor of psychology and inclusion at the University of Bristol, Dr Nilu Ahmed.

"You've got a set amount of time so you know what you can do. You know that it's going to come to an end. So you're not going to go on a rampage and riot out in the streets. You know that it's going to be contained."

But Ahmed said it can't replace long term therapy.

"For deep rooted issues, it's going to come up again and again. And the question that I always talk about is where are those feelings being discussed?

"And if they are being taken into a rage room, what that is telling the individual or telling me as a professional, is that individual hasn't got a safe space to go and talk about that."

For Ellie, smashing Ryan's possessions did not take away the loss.

But she says it gave her an hour to channel her grief, remember her brother and leave feeling lighter than when she arrived.

articles.title: What is next for Israel?
articles.summary: The message of the vote is that the violent Israeli policies within occupied territory and the region will continue.
articles.body:
There are two ways to read the results of the Israeli elections. One way would be to see them as a defeat for the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. From holding a solid majority in the 120-member Knesset, the Netanyahu bloc has been reduced to a minority of 53 members. Anti-Netanyahu lawmakers, by contrast, hold 67 seats.

Had Israel been a democracy, we would have seen scenes of celebration similar to the ones we saw this year in Hungary, Brazil and Serbia, where political forces with undemocratic tendencies were defeated. But Israel is not a democracy, and Netanyahu was not necessarily defeated.

The second, more relevant way of reading the results of the Israeli election would necessitate accepting the apartheid nature of Israel and seeing the electoral arithmetic through that prism. In this case, Netanyahu won because he secured 53 seats in the Knesset – five more than the anti-Netanyahu Jewish bloc.

To form a government, a bloc needs to have the support of at least 61 members of the Knesset. The only way Netanyahu can do it is by enticing parties or lawmakers from the anti-Netanyahu bloc to join his bloc, as he has succeeded in doing many times in the past. Working with Palestinian parties, which secured 19 seats, is out of the question for him.

The obvious path for government formation for the anti-Netanyahu bloc would be to form a coalition – one that would include the two Palestinian parties. But to do so would mean to challenge Israeli apartheid. The main leaders of the Jewish anti-Netanyahu bloc, including Gadi Eisenkot, have promised not to do so under any circumstances.

There is another option: seeking the support of the religious Orthodox parties, which have so far been part of the Netanyahu bloc. To secure their backing, the anti-Netanyahu bloc would have to promise to exempt religious Orthodox youth from military service and guarantee funding for their learning centres.

However, Eisenkot’s main election promise was forcing young Haredi Jews into the army. So this is not a very likely scenario, but in politics, never say never.

There is also the option of a “unity government” led by some sort of rotation between the leading figures of the anti-Netanyahu bloc and Netanyahu. The problem here is that, according to a law passed a few years ago, as long as Netanyahu is still a defendant in an ongoing trial, he cannot serve as a minister; his coalition made sure that the legislation ridiculously would not apply to a prime minister.

Given that Netanyahu’s corruption trial is destined to go on for a very long time, the rotation would make it impossible for Netanyahu to be part of a government under Eisenkot as prime minister. That means he would demand to hold the rotating premiership first and leave open the option to collapse the government once his rotation is over.

Netanyahu has already done that before. In 2020, without any hesitation, he broke a rotation agreement with Benny Gantz, who had naively believed that after two years he would be the prime minister. This resulted in new elections, which Netanyahu won.

Finally, a very possible scenario is that neither of the two blocs would be able to form a government, which would mean new elections in six months. Netanyahu and his government would remain in office until the new polls, albeit with more limited authority.

This would give them the opportunity to reignite a war with Iran and Hezbollah and continue with their violent policies in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank in an attempt to attract more public support and win the elections.

This is the preferred option for Netanyahu because his relative defeat in the October 27 elections had a lot to do with the unprecedented galvanisation among the Palestinian voters in Israel and the more liberal Jewish Israelis living abroad who came back home in huge numbers to vote.

These possible scenarios tell only part of the story and are not enough to fully understand what the election results mean for Israel, the Palestinians and the region. Here are the more important conclusions one should draw from the results:

The first pertains to the future of the Palestinian citizens of Israel. They still could turn out to vote in large numbers if new elections are held soon. But if they are once more ignored and sidelined by the other political parties, they will never try it again.

In this case, it would be difficult for the leadership of this community to continue to delay a strategic decision: choosing which political space Palestinian citizens of Israel belong to – the Israeli or the Palestinian one?

Until today, they have given a chance to the Israeli political system despite its racism, apartheid tendencies and criminal policies towards Palestinians. Palestinian parties recommended Eisenkot for the premiership to President Isaac Herzog, who has now tasked him with forming a government.

If I can venture a prediction – and it is only a prediction – the anti-Netanyahu bloc would not engage meaningfully with the Palestinian parties. Its message, therefore, will be that the Palestinians of Israel are not legitimate players in the Israeli political field.

If I am wrong, this would be an incredible and transformative moment in the history of both Israel and Palestine, but there seems to be very little hope for such a development.

There are other lessons we can learn from where we are now with the knowledge that this is a very volatile moment in the history of Israel.

The first and most important one is that whoever forms the next government of Israel will continue the incremental genocide in Gaza, the intensified ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and the aggressive policies towards the region. These policies as before can only be stopped or tamed by the region and the international community sending a clear message to Israel that there will be a price tag attached to such policies.

The second lesson is that the Israeli Jewish society is as deeply divided as ever, to the point that it is impossible for it to maintain a stable political system, a thriving economy and a positive strategy towards the region and the world.

The third lesson is that Israel’s international isolation will increase as a result of this trajectory, including the continued dissociation from Zionism among young Jews around the world, including in the United States.

Finally and most importantly, this can have an impact on the global discussion about Zionism. The move by the Green Party in Britain to define Zionism as racism – despite being currently an exception and widely condemned – will gain validity with time.

These elections and future developments are making clear that Zionism in the current Israeli politics means the exclusion of Palestinian citizens of Israel from politics – first by ignoring them and quite possibly in the future by denying them the right to vote

Moreover, many in the international community will associate the term Zionism with a consensual Israeli policy of genocide, ethnic cleansing and apartheid.

The outlook in the short term is worrying. The overall message from the Israeli elections is that the future policies of the state will continue to threaten the lives of the Palestinians in occupied territory, Palestinian citizens of Israel, and the people of southern Lebanon and Syria. There will be more instability in the region.

In the long run, however, as bad as it is, the fundamental cracks in the Zionist project will widen, which might lead to its demise. One can only hope this will also lead to the beginning of a political reality that would benefit everyone who lives in historical Palestine and the region.

A version of this oped was first published by Al Jazeera Arabic .

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Whiskey dates & billion-dollar deals: How Nvidia boss Jensen Huang landed in Chinese spy scandal
articles.summary: Alice Huang, a Chinese business executive suspected by US intelligence of working for Beijing, allegedly developed an intimate relationship with Nvidia
articles.body: Alice Huang, a Chinese business executive suspected by US intelligence of working for Beijing, allegedly developed an intimate relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, raising concerns that one of America's most influential technology executives may have been targeted in a Chinese espionage operation. Huang, is believed to have been recruited by China's intelligence apparatus to gather information about the billionaire and potentially influence his decisions on the global artificial intelligence industry.The allegations have placed the Nvidia chief, 63, under renewed scrutiny, with reports suggesting that US intelligence agencies had identified the suspected operation well before it became public.Also read: Who is Alice Huang? Chinese businesswoman at centre of Nvidia spy scandalA report by the Financial Times said American officials had prepared a classified memo detailing the alleged romantic relationship. The development adds a new dimension to earlier revelations by The New York Times, which first reported that Huang had developed a close relationship with the Chinese businesswoman.What we knowAlice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen with reported connections across the global AI chip industry.According to the Daily Mail, the two allegedly became romantically involved, with US intelligence officials suspecting that the relationship could have been part of a Chinese espionage operation. The Financial Times reportedly revealed that American agencies had prepared a classified assessment of their alleged intimacy, which was circulated among a small group of senior government officials.Their association reportedly dates back to at least June 2024, when they were photographed together at a bar in Taipei following a technology trade show. Images shared on LinkedIn by technology company NetThunder showed Huang, wearing his trademark black leather jacket, sitting alongside Alice Huang during an evening gathering with industry executives. The two were reportedly seen drinking whiskey.They appeared together again in May 2025 at a dinner hosted by the Nvidia chief at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, a major technology exhibition. Photographs and livestream footage showed Alice Huang sitting close to him, kissing him on the cheek and putting her hand on his back. She was also seen following him when he stepped outside to speak to journalists. The two later left the restaurant in the same car.Who is Alice Huang and what is Megaspeed's China connection?Alice Huang reportedly worked as a television journalist in China before moving into the technology sector. An online profile on a Chinese fund database, which AFP said it could not independently verify, listed previous employment at HSBC and Chinese broadcasters CCTV and Hunan TV.She later became a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that rents computing power to businesses for training and running AI systems. The company's website describes it as a core business partner of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.According to the New York Times, Megaspeed had been under US government scrutiny since 2024 over suspicions that it was helping channel restricted Nvidia processors into China. Singapore authorities also reportedly questioned Alice Huang in 2025 as part of an investigation into the company.The Daily Mail reported that Megaspeed was spun off from a Chinese gaming company and expanded into AI data centres. The New York Times also reported that it had purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over two years.Washington restricts exports of its most advanced AI processors to China over concerns that the technology could strengthen Beijing's military and technological capabilities. Megaspeed denied allegations of illegal chip transfers in December 2025, describing Bloomberg's reporting on the matter as misleading. Nvidia has also previously said its investigations found no evidence of wrongdoing.What Jensen Huang saidIn his statement, the Nvidia chief apologised to his family for being unfaithful and said that the supported the independent investigation launched by the Nvidia board.What Jensen Huang wrote:To my colleagues at NVIDIA,I owe my family and all of you an apology.I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.JensenYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: The $500 million gamble to make India’s ‘Ramayana’ a global phenomenon
articles.summary: Can a Hindu epic become the world’s next great movie franchise? Filmmaker Namit Malhotra is about to find out.
articles.body: Namit Malhotra looks awfully relaxed for a man taking a $500 million gamble. Reclining into a sofa in a discreet London office, the movie producer bats away questions about the box office potential and estimated price tag of his two-part blockbuster adaptation of the Hindu epic, “The Ramayana.” “I’m not motivated by the bean-counter logic of, ‘How much money did we make or not make,” he said. “If we don’t make money with the movies, we’ll make it in the merchandise. If we don’t make it in the merchandise, we’ll make it in the theme park. If we don’t make it in the theme park, we’ll make it some other way. “This is the story of Lord Ram, OK? There is no version of this where people don’t like (the movies) and it does not drive economic upside.” “The Ramayana” — or at least this version of it (there are hundreds) — tells the story of Rama, a divine prince who answers the call to defeat Ravana, a demon king whose ambition and power threatened the gods themselves. The source text is a more than 2,000-year-old epic poem, attributed to Hindu sage Valmiki, which recounts a cosmic Manichean battle with a list of heroes longer than “Avengers: Doomsday.” It’s a story that generations of Indians have grown up on, and one that has been adapted many times before, including a beloved 1980s TV serial that ran for over a year. But the epic has never been told on this scale, nor with a global audience in mind. I first met Malhotra in spring, months out from last Thursday’s release of part one, “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.” He is the CEO of eight-time Oscar-winning British visual effects studio DNEG and founder of Mumbai-based Prime Focus Studios. Talkative and patriotic, Malhotra is a third-generation filmmaker gunning to expand India’s cinematic clout and redefine what audiences think about films from the world’s most populous country. And, unlike most in the movie business, he’s fronting his dream with his own cash. “It’s all my money,” he said. “I have all the risk … I’m going all in.” “Ramayana” is the most expensive Indian film production ever, though an average of $250 million per film puts it in the same ballpark as your typical Marvel movie (or some of the more profligate efforts by streaming giants). However, the most money an Indian film has ever made at the global box office is $304 million — 2016’s “Dangal,” starring Aamir Khan. Factor in “Ramayana’s” globe-hopping marketing campaign and the odds appear stacked against it recouping costs in cinemas. But with the potential wild card of an (as-yet-confirmed) box office release in China — where “Dangal” grossed 64% of its global take — anything is possible. Malhotra has leveraged his little black book to realize this passion project. He hired “Dangal” director Nitesh Tiwari to write and direct both parts. He cast lead actors from across India’s multilingual cinema industries: Hindi star Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Kannada-speaking actor Yash as Ravana, and Tamil and Teluga star Sai Pallavi as Rama’s wife Sita. He also recruited the cream of Hollywood’s craft departments to bring his vision to life, and half of Bollywood to build it. He asked Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman to buddy up on the score and put DNEG — whose credits this year include “The Odyssey” and “Dune: Part Three” — in charge of visual effects. “It should be mounted with the resources and the stars and the director and music like any big Hollywood tentpole,” said Malhotra. “Because until we do that, we will always be the have-nots. We will always feel like we tried and we didn’t get there.” Part one was shot mostly on soundstages in Mumbai. As one might expect for a story featuring a flying palace, demon warriors and a winged elephant, Airavata, the film is an CGI-heavy spectacle. “I’ve never done a movie which had so much visual effects,” said Yash, who also co-produced. The special effect that has made the most headlines is the AI-assisted lip-synced dubbing, from Hindi to English, for the international release. Malhotra said the actors recorded their lines in English and that their voices aren’t AI generated. But a combination of motion capture and AI was used to match mouth and facial movements to the new speech. Overseeing the process was Brahma AI, an Indian tech company valued at $2 billion that is part of DNEG Group. “It’s taken us over a year, and millions of dollars spent” to make the English dub, said Malhotra. Internationally, “Ramayana” is being billed as India’s answer to “Avatar” or “The Lord of the Rings.” One fundamental difference is that it is a religious narrative. “We ourselves are believers,” said Tiwari, speaking of his and Malhotra’s shared Hindu faith. “When you have (the) sensibilities of billions of people attached to an epic, you have to tread very cautiously,” he said. Tiwari explained that the screenplay is based on the two most popular versions of the Ramayana, and included elements from others too. “But everything is from the scriptures,” he clarified. Films inspired by the Ramayana are not guaranteed slam drunks. Just three years ago, big-budget action film “Adipurush” bombed at the box office amid public backlash. Malhotra’s “Ramayana” will face intense scrutiny by India’s cinemagoers, and all eyes are on Kapoor as Rama, an idealized hero broadly worshipped by Hindus. The Bollywood star, first known for romantic comedies, and recently action dramas, said the responsibility was “daunting” and that he was reluctant to take on Rama. “There is a certain professional and personal baggage that I come with,” Kapoor explained. “People have been seeing me on screen for the last 18 years playing different parts.” “I didn’t have confidence in myself,” he admitted. “Will I be able to fit the part? Will I be able to do justice to it? Will the audience accept me? There will always be a conversation, like, ‘He’s not fit to play this part.’” Kapoor said “sense prevailed” and he signed on. “I don’t think I will ever, ever get (another) opportunity like this to tell a story like this. It’s not about the money spent, or the fact that it was going to be a global film. It’s just being a part of a story which we worship. Our value systems, our moral codes have been derived from these stories.” “Ramayana” arrives amid a recent wave of big-screen adaptations of ancient epics and mythology. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” based on Homer’s epic, drew audiences to theaters this summer, while Chinese animation “Ne Zha 2,” inspired by Chinese mythology, became the world’s highest-grossing movie of 2025. The latter grossed $2.2 billion in China alone, aided by a Lunar New Year release and reports that companies booked screenings for employees and subsidized tickets. Part one of “Ramayana” was released just days before Diwali, which is associated with Rama’s return home from exile. The filmmakers will have been hoping to seize on the celebratory mood, and are pitching the movie to the whole nation, not just the Hindi-speaking population. Some of the creative decisions have been calculated to broaden appeal. “Ramayana is every Indian’s story,” said Malhotra, explaining why he cast actors from across the country. “What was very important was for us to really make it feel like (the film is) from India first; that it’s not from Bollywood.” Joyojeet Pal, professor of information at the University of Michigan, saw sense in touting the movie as an industry unifier. “It is important to do that, because a lot of the discourse around the spate of nationalistic films out right now is that they present a sectarian view of India that tends to be dominated by a North Indian, Hindu-oriented narrative,” he explained. “There is another, more complicated side to the narrative in that the main antagonist of the dominant version of ‘The Ramayana,’ Ravana, is seen as a heroic character in parts of the south,” Pal added. “Thus, presenting a pan-Indian narrative is valuable as part of its branding.” Yash predicted lively scenes in Indian movie theaters come opening weekend. “I think it’ll turn into a stadium there, or like a music concert,” he said. “There is a collective experience that (Indian audiences) all want to feel at the cinemas,” added Kapoor. “They root for you; at the same time, when you disappoint them, they will also criticize you. And we love that. We love the fact that they have the ability to do both. The power is in the audience’s hands. “It’s a dream job to be an actor in Indian cinema, and we hope that we can continue being actors and continue to be accepted there,” he said. How “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” will be received abroad, and if it can surpass diaspora appeal, will be its biggest test. “In India we love world cinema,” said Pallavi. “So, it’ll be nice if it’s (the other way) around.” The film grossed more $55 million globally on its opening weekend, including $12.2 million in the US, according to Deadline. While it now appears unlikely that “Ramayana” will beat Hindi record-breaker “Dhurandhar: The Revenge,” which grossed $115.3 million worldwide in its first week March, it is nonetheless on course to join India’s highest grossing movies of all time. Back in Malhotra’s office earlier this year, the producer had been buoyant. “I don’t want to sound spiritual as a businessman,” he said. “But honestly … you can’t do this right and not succeed.” “To me, there’s one fundamental truth: that if we do ‘Ramayana’ well, and if people like it, financially we’ll be fine,” he added. “That’s my fundamental belief. There’s no way to argue it. There’s no way to debate it. And I don’t think anybody in the world is smart enough to counter it with scientific or commercial logic.”

articles.title: Man accused of killing 6 in far-right shooting rampage dies in hospital, Polish police say
articles.summary: The man who opened fire in a public square, killing six people in a suspected far-right terror attack in Kraków, Poland, has died, police said early Monday.
articles.body: The man who opened fire in a public square, killing six people in a suspected far-right terror attack in Kraków, Poland, has died, police said early Monday. The man, 24, was shot by police during Saturday’s midday rampage in Main Market Square, the historic center of Poland’s second-largest city. More than a dozen others, including two police officers, were injured. The two officers were in “serious” condition, regional official Krzysztof Jan Klęczar said Sunday. The gunman “acted with the aim of seriously intimidating a large number of people, making this a terrorist offence,” Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said on X. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said he used an automatic rifle to carry out the attack and that he “was fascinated by far-right ideologies.” However, officials appeared to backtrack from the earlier comments as nationalist opposition politicians questioned the grounds on which the interior minister had said far-right ideology was the motive. “Until the matter is fully clarified and the authorities are in possession of complete information, it is best to refrain from making comments, even if there are some initial indications,” government spokesman Adam Szlapka told TVN24. Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said on Monday that despite the death of the shooter, the investigation will continue, aiming to establish if he acted alone or was inspired by any group. “Evidence is being collected, but I will not show or disclose it. I ask for restraint,” Zurek told Radio Zet. A man and two women, believed to be the shooter’s parents and sister, were also found dead in an apartment in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyskie, a city about 93 miles northeast of Kraków, according to Andrzej Fijołek, deputy inspector of Police National Headquarters. The suspect faced murder charges in those killings, as well, Żurek said Sunday. Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, authorities said. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead. The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon. Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria. The attack took place in Kraków’s popular commerce and tourist destination. “We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around,” Marie-Ange Collaer, who was visiting with her family from Brussels, wrote on Facebook.

articles.title: Triple murder in Tamil Nadu: 2 teens hacked to death, IT employee killed on Diwali night
articles.summary: TIRUCHIRAPPALLI: Three people, including two 17-year-old boys, were allegedly murdered in separate incidents in Tamil Nadu's Tiruchirappalli district on
articles.body: TIRUCHIRAPPALLI: Three people, including two 17-year-old boys, were allegedly murdered in separate incidents in Tamil Nadu's Tiruchirappalli district on Diwali, leaving residents shocked.In the first incident, two teenagers were hacked to death by unidentified assailants near the Samayapuram toll plaza on the outskirts of Tiruchirappalli.In a separate incident near Irungalur, a 20-year-old Chennai-based IT company employee was allegedly stabbed to death with an iron spanner following an argument over bursting firecrackers.Trichy district police said Rahul (17), a resident of Inam Samayapuram, had lost both his parents and was living with a relative while working as a daily wage labourer. His relative's brother, Vishal (17), also worked as a daily wage labourer.According to news agency ANI, the two were walking along the Pullambadi canal near the Dhanalakshmi Srinivasan University campus, close to the Samayapuram toll plaza, at around 11.30pm on Diwali night when a group of unidentified men allegedly attacked them with sharp weapons.Vishal suffered severe injuries to his face, while Rahul sustained multiple cut injuries to his head and neck. Both were found lying in a pool of blood.Passersby alerted the Samayapuram police, who rushed to the spot. Vishal was found dead at the scene, while Rahul also succumbed to his injuries before he could be shifted to the hospital.The bodies were recovered and sent to Tiruchirappalli Government Hospital for post-mortem examination.Tiruchirappalli district Superintendent of Police Dongare Praveen Umesh visited the crime scene and reviewed the investigation. Forensic experts collected evidence, while police scanned CCTV footage from nearby areas.On the SP's instructions, three special teams have been formed to identify and trace the accused. Police are also investigating whether the murders were linked to past enmity or a revenge motive.In another incident, Christopher (20), a native of Purathakudi near Irungalur in Mannachanallur taluk, was allegedly murdered following a dispute over bursting firecrackers.Christopher, son of Xavier Lawrence, worked with a private IT company in Chennai and had returned to his native village for the Diwali holidays.On Diwali evening, he was bursting firecrackers with his friends Ranjith (26) and Lenin (21) on Middle Street in Purathakudi.At that time, three men identified as Donald, Edison and Charles, residents of the same locality, allegedly questioned them over bursting firecrackers in their direction, leading to an argument.The argument soon escalated into a physical altercation. During the clash, Donald allegedly picked up an iron spanner and attacked Christopher on the left side of his chest and Ranjith on his face.Both injured men were rushed to Dhanalakshmi Srinivasan Medical College Hospital in Samayapuram. However, doctors declared Christopher dead, reportedly due to severe injuries to his heart region. Ranjith is undergoing treatment.The Samayapuram police recovered Christopher's body and sent it to Tiruchirappalli Government Hospital for post-mortem examination.A case has been registered, and police are searching for the three accused, who are reportedly absconding.The Lalgudi Deputy Superintendent of Police visited the spot and directed the deployment of more than 20 police personnel to prevent further incidents.The three murders reported at different locations in Tiruchirappalli district on Diwali have triggered shock and grief among residents. articles.title: Native American women made history in tribal, state and federal elections
articles.summary: The win marks a turning point for Native American women, whose leadership in their families and communities has rarely translated to formal political power.
articles.body: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. — A third-grade field trip to the Navajo Nation Council sparked Crystalyne Curley’s political ambition when she witnessed a fiery debate erupt between two tribal lawmakers. “I thought to myself at a very young age, that’s where I want to be,” Curley said. On Election Day, Curley surpassed that childhood dream and broke a barrier she says she never imagined as a nine-year-old: She was elected the first woman president of the Navajo Nation. This week’s elections brought a wave of milestone victories, from the nation’s first Black female governor to the first openly gay man and first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. It also marked a turning point for Native American women, whose leadership in their families and communities has rarely translated to formal political power. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the Senate, Deb Haaland the first to win a state governorship, and Curley the first to lead one of the largest tribes. “This is a win for all Navajo women,” Curley told The Associated Press. Jordan James Harvill, a Cherokee Nation citizen and strategist with the advocacy group Advance Native Political Leadership, said decades of political organizing are bearing fruit as more Native women run for and win office. “This is a seismic shift that is happening in our communities,” he said. The Navajo Nation elects its first woman president Lene Bitsui supported Curley in the Navajo Nation election because she felt she was best positioned to restore order to the tribal government after what she sees as a period of dysfunction. But when Bitsui cast her ballot, she felt pessimistic. “I thought our people weren’t ready for a female president,” Bitsui said. “I was wrong, and I feel so happy to have been wrong.” The modern, centralized Navajo government has been led by men since its establishment under federal pressure over a century ago. Navajo has the largest land base of any federally recognized tribe, spanning 27,000 square miles (70,000 square kilometers) in Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is second in population to the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma. Some Navajo people believe traditional teachings prohibit women from holding top government positions. Others say women’s absence from the presidency stands in contrast to the matrilineal structure of Diné society. “You see the language of tradition used to both deride the possibility of a woman being president and to say that women’s leadership is needed now,” said Jennifer Nez Denetdale, a professor of Diné studies at the University of New Mexico. Curley, who narrowly defeated attorney Justin Jones, according to unofficial results, told the AP she faced sexist rhetoric while campaigning and expects to be held to a higher standard as the first woman president. “As women, we have to work twice or triple as hard, especially within Navajo politics,” said Curley, who also was the first female to lead the tribe’s legislative branch as speaker of the tribal council. After Curley and her running mate Chris Deschene take office in January, they plan to transition the Navajo Nation away from coal development, historically a major economic engine for the tribe, and reassert its leading role in national discussions around federal Indian policy. The Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York also elected its first woman president, longtime council member Tina Abrams, on Tuesday. Native women make gains in U.S. Congress At her Senate victory celebration in St. Paul, Minnesota, Democrat Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation and the state’s outgoing lieutenant governor, credited supporters from her community. “I could not run for the U. S. Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women,” Flanagan said. More than 230 years after the U.S. Senate was established, only four Native people have served in the chamber, all men. “This is a win that shows we can break every single glass ceiling,” Harvill said. Flanagan will join Oklahoma Republican Sen. Tom Cole, a citizen of the Chickasaw Nation. A victory for Democrat Mary Peltola, a Yup’ik woman, in Alaska’s still unsettled Senate race, would mark the first time three Native people have served in the chamber simultaneously. In the House, Kansas Democrat Sharice Davids, Ho-Chunk, and Oklahoma Republican Josh Brecheen, Choctaw, won reelection. New York Democrat Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, and Michigan Democrat Sean McCann, a citizen of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, became the first Native Americans elected to represent their states in Congress. Deb Haaland notches another first in New Mexico Haaland’s political career has been defined by historic milestones. She was one of the first two Native women elected to Congress in 2018 before becoming the first Native American to lead a U.S. Cabinet agency, the Interior Department. Now, in her home state of New Mexico, the Laguna Pueblo citizen, will break ground as the first female Native governor of a U.S. state. “I think it’s a long time coming,” said Haaland, who traces her ancestry in what is now New Mexico back 800 years. She is tasked with making good on campaign promises to make life more affordable for struggling New Mexicans and addressing persistently poor education outcomes in the state. Haaland, who is affectionately known as “Auntie Deb” in parts of Indian Country, was tearful reflecting on the support she has received from Native voters and other Native women in politics, including Davids and Flanagan. “It makes me very happy that we’re able to have a presence,” Haaland said. “It’s not just a slogan. It matters that people feel represented.”

articles.title: A Vadodara engineer left his corporate career in 2012 to take travellers beyond hotels and into villages; 14 years later, Chirag Munjani's rural travel venture runs 70 to 80 trips a year across 16 to 17 destinations
articles.summary: For many, a holiday means checking into a premium hotel, enjoying the views and visiting famous landmarks.
articles.body: For many, a holiday means checking into a premium hotel, enjoying the views and visiting famous landmarks. Returning home with memories and photographs is the best part of it. But what if a journey could offer something more meaningful, something more to remember by? That’s exactly what Chirag Munjani, an engineer from Vadodara, Gujarat, has been trying to introduce to Indian travellers for over a decade now.Chirag left his corporate career in 2012 to create a venture around rural and experiential tourism. Fourteen years later, his initiative, Rural Pleasure Journeys, organises around 70 to 80 trips annually across 16 to 17 destinations, taking travellers into villages, forests and communities that conventional tourism often overlooks.Meet Chirah MunjaniBorn and based in Vadodara, Munjani studied mechanical engineering at Gujarat University. He then went on pursuing an MBA from the Symbiosis Institute of Business Management in Pune, which he completed in 2004.In June 2004 he joined Bajaj Auto as a management trainee. Over the years, he worked with Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Auto Finance. However, his corporate assignments exposed him to a side of India that most conventional travellers rarely encounter.While working in rural markets, Munjani frequently travelled to remote locations and interacted with people and communities outside the usual urban business environment. Talking to The Indian Express, he recalled how his work in rural areas made him realise that there was an opportunity to introduce travellers to destinations through their people, heritage and ecology.In 2012, he set up Rural Pleasure Journeys, a Vadodara-based travel venture focused on rural and experiential tourism. His philosophy was different from conventional sightseeing. Instead of taking visitors from one attraction to another, he wanted them to understand the places they visited.Taking travellers inside the villagesOne of the most interesting aspects of his venture was connecting visitors with local livelihoods. For example, a trip to the Little Rann of Kutch offers travellers an opportunity to understand salt production.Salt is something most households use every day, yet few people know where it comes from or how it is produced. Through these experiences, visitors get an opportunity to understand the hard work and traditional knowledge that go into making an everyday essential.The idea is taking tourism beyond sightseeing and towards conservation. His approach also extends to community participation and environmental conservation.But introducing it in Dang, which is among Gujarat's poorest districts, was difficult because forest regulations restrict several commercial activities in the region. Initially, convincing tribal communities to welcome outsiders was a challenge.Working for wildlifeThe venture has also developed experiences around wildlife conservation near Gir National Park. Lions sometimes fall into open wells in agricultural areas while chasing prey. As part of conservation-linked activities, visitors can participate in efforts to make protective grills for these wells, including learning about and taking part in fabrication work.From one idea to 80 trips a yearOver the years, the geographical footprint also expanded. While it initially focused on Gujarat, it entered Madhya Pradesh in 2023 and Rajasthan in 2024.Today, they offer both fixed and customised itineraries across 16 to 17 destinations and organise approximately 70 to 80 trips every year, with local communities involved at each destination.For Munjani, the idea of travel has always been about creating connections that go beyond photographs and sightseeing. For him, a visit to a village can introduce someone to an artisan's lifelong craft. A journey through a salt-producing region can make an everyday ingredient feel entirely different. And an experience around Gir can help visitors understand why protecting wildlife also means supporting the communities living alongside it.Fourteen years after taking that leap, his venture is helping travellers discover an India that often remains outside conventional itineraries. articles.title: Floods bring rare relief to U.S. Southwest reservoirs as Lake Powell rises 20 feet
articles.summary: Recent flooding across the U.S. Southwest is providing rare relief to thirsty reservoirs that had fallen to record lows amid a yearslong megadrought.
articles.body: PHOENIX — Recent flooding across the U.S. Southwest is providing rare relief to thirsty reservoirs that had fallen to record lows amid a yearslong megadrought. Storms in late October and early November sent torrents of water through normally small or dry creeks that overflowed their banks and flooded local communities. Hundreds of people were told to evacuate, and the flooding cut off access to some areas. Yet most of that water will end up feeding depleted lakes and underground aquifers, said Martin Hoerling, a climate scientist and hydrologist at the University of Colorado, Boulder. “That’s somewhat of an unexpected boost from Mother Nature,” Hoerling said. Last winter’s lackluster snowfall did little to recharge water bodies when it melted in the spring and summer, when they typically get their biggest bump of the year. Then came the chaotic climate phenomenon, El Niño, that has intensified heavy rain and floods. Experts say its impacts will last several more months, potentially further boosting water supplies across the West where water primarily is stored in lakes, aquifers and snowpack. Lake Powell, the second-largest reservoir in the U.S., rose more than 20 feet (6.1 meters) from its mid-September low — dwarfing its gains from this year’s snowmelt, Hoerling said. Still, the lake remained just over a quarter full, and 15 of its 17 boat launches remained unusable as of Friday. The floodwaters and additional rain could raise the lake along the Arizona-Utah border further, for a total of over 1.2 million acre-feet — enough to support around 4 million average families for a year, Hoerling estimated. Rain brings temporary relief to regional and local water supplies Cities in the region reported some of their wettest weather in decades. Before storms began dumping about 7 inches (17.78 centimeters) of rain around Pagosa Springs, Colorado, in October, more than 10,000 people in the town and surrounding communities were under water restrictions. Restaurants were encouraged to serve water only on request, town manager David Harris said. Those restrictions are now lifted. “While the storm was destructive, I think there is a silver lining,” Harris said. “You’re getting a good start to the winter snowpack in the higher elevations.” Upper Lake Mary, which captures spring snowmelt in Northern Arizona and supplies Flagstaff, Arizona, with up to 40% of its water, received more than 3 billion gallons of water since early October, said Flagstaff water production manager Brian Huntzinger. Storms last weekend dumped the equivalent of more than two years of water into the town’s surface water supply and provided a buffer for an operation that depends heavily on underground aquifers, Huntzinger said. “It’s just a great, great thing to see,” Huntzinger said. “We might be overflowing at this rate before we see any snow fly.” In central Arizona, heavy floodwaters that trapped people in their homes gushed into streams that feed the Verde River. That prompted water officials to release water from two nearly full dams into the Verde’s normally dry stretch in metro Phoenix, said Bo Svoma, the principal meteorologist at the Salt River Project that manages reservoirs on the Salt and Verde rivers. Wet weather is unlikely to change decisions on the Colorado River The region remains in drought despite the intense rains. And decisions already have been made to divvy up water in the Colorado River basin. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, which manages reservoirs in the West, is unlikely to change its water releases from Lake Powell or other areas until it knows when snowpack has peaked, typically around April, said Jack Schmidt, a Utah State University professor who studies the Colorado River. Reclamation spokesperson Mary Carlson acknowledged conditions have improved but added ”considerable uncertainty remains.” Under the federal plan for managing the Colorado River’s Lower Basin, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet (about 1.54 billion cubic meters) annually in the next two years. That is enough to fill over 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions. Nevada and Arizona are challenging the plan in court. Some Arizona cities have agreed to fund preliminary work to reduce reliance on the Colorado River by expanding an existing dam on the Verde River to capture runoff from storms, Svoma said. “We need to figure out how to be resilient in a drier future. And we’re not quite there yet,” Hoerling said.
